catalog_quote: The minimal sets from (17) to (31) prove that there are two tonemes in Kokborok. 44 represents the high tone and 22 represents the low tone in all the data. ... Low tone is the unmarked tone in Kokborok as the majority of the lexical items carry this tone, whereas the high tone is considered as the marked tone. ... Similar to Bodo, Kokborok also has two tonemes namely, high and low. The marked tone is the high tone in Kokborok. ... In comparing with the other Bodo-Garo languages, Kokborok vowels and tones are closely related to Bodo, Dimasa, Rabha, and Tiwa. new_statements.quote: Considering the Kokbrorok tonal pattern and the previous works on tones for Bodo-Garo languages (Sarmah & Wiltshire 2009, Joseph & Burling 2001), it can be generalized that in disyllabic words, the tones (low or high) are only assigned in the second syllable whereas in first syllable a default tone (mid/level) is present in Bodo-Garo languages. The reason for this in Kokborok is that, in disyllabic words, the stress is always on the second syllable. Similar pattern in Bodo and Dimasa were also noticed in disyllabic words

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kokborok is a two-tone language (high vs. low, low unmarked); in disyllabic words the lexical tone contrast is realised on the second syllable, which is also the stressed syllable, the first syllable carrying a default mid/level pitch. I.e. non-initial (second = final in disyllables) prominence; nothing is said about words of three or more syllables. Supporting older statement (Chakraborty 1981: 16, Bengali): Tipra stress is unlike English/Bengali word stress; it falls on the group-final vowel when that vowel is a tense suffix, case ending or particle, and is otherwise used word-specifically to separate near-homophones.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Veikho & Mushahary. Chakraborty 1981: 16 mentions word-specific (initial) stress used to disambiguate near-homophones, e.g. butui 'egg' vs butui 'broth'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is explicitly limited to disyllabic words (elicited citation forms, 5 speakers of the Debbarma/standard variety); stress is invoked to explain tone alignment, not measured itself. Reading 'fixed: final syllable' is provisional: for disyllables 'second' and 'final' coincide; Chakraborty's remark that suffix/particle-final vowels take the stress and the Bodo-Garo rightmost-tone pattern favour final over 'second'.
new_statements.identity_note: Veikho & Mushahary 2015 recorded 5 speakers of the Debbarma (standard/Agartala) variety of Kokborok = kokb1239. Chakraborty 1981 describes 'Tipra' (= Kokborok/Tripuri, same language). Sheela Debbarma 2021 covers Debbarma standard plus Reang (rian1250? = Riang [ria], a separate Glottolog languoid) and Jamatia dialects; her tone data are not used for the statement.

sources.quote: Considering the Kokbrorok tonal pattern and the previous works on tones for Bodo-Garo languages (Sarmah & Wiltshire 2009, Joseph & Burling 2001), it can be generalized that in disyllabic words, the tones (low or high) are only assigned in the second syllable whereas in first syllable a default tone (mid/level) is present in Bodo-Garo languages. The reason for this in Kokborok is that, in disyllabic words, the stress is always on the second syllable. Similar pattern in Bodo and Dimasa were also noticed in disyllabic words
sources.note: p.166 (conclusion): tones are assigned only to the second syllable of disyllables because 'in disyllabic words, the stress is always on the second syllable'; two tonemes (high marked, low unmarked); Debbarma (standard) variety, 5 speakers.

sources.note: pp.15-16: Tipra has both tone (4 pitch patterns claimed) and stress (jhonk); stress is 'not like English or Bengali stress'; it falls (1) word-specifically, e.g. initial stress on butui 'egg' to keep it apart from butui 'broth', and (2) on the final vowel of a breath-group when that vowel belongs to a tense suffix, case ending or particle. Page image (leaf 28 = p.16) saved and checked against scanned.
